opus-5.5.text:
Language has always struck me as this unusually good window into what's going on inside people's heads. Most of cognition is hidden from us; we can't directly observe how someone represents the world, how they plan, or how they reason about other people. But when people talk, they're externalizing a lot of that. Language is the medium we use to share knowledge, coordinate, teach each other, and describe what we believe and want. So if you want to understand the structure of thought, studying how meaning gets packed into words and sentences, and unpacked again by a listener, seems like one of the most direct handles you can get.

There's also a nice methodological reason. Language is a domain where you have both rich data and a lot of existing theory. Linguists, philosophers, and psychologists have spent a long time thinking carefully about compositionality, reference, and pragmatics: how we get from a finite vocabulary to an unbounded space of meanings, and how context shapes what someone is actually trying to communicate. That gives you concrete hypotheses to test computationally. You can build a model, ask whether it captures those phenomena, and when it fails, the failures are often informative about what the underlying cognitive machinery has to look like.

And I think the past several years have made this even more interesting. We now have systems that learn from enormous amounts of text and end up doing surprisingly sophisticated things. That raises real scientific questions: what kinds of representations of the world can you actually acquire just from language? Do these models build anything like the structured models of situations, agents, and beliefs that we think humans use? Studying them gives us a new kind of experimental object. We can intervene on their internals in ways we never could with people, and that lets us sharpen questions about cognition that used to be mostly philosophical.

So for me it's always been a two-way street. Language is a lens on human cognition, and building machines that use language is both a way of testing our theories about that cognition and, hopefully, a way of building tools that can learn from and communicate with people more naturally.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that I came to it a little bit backwards. I was interested in language first, and the cognitive science angle grew out of that. But the reason it stuck, the reason I kept thinking language was the right lens, is that language is the one place where we get to actually see the structure of thought written out in a form we can study.

If you want to understand how people represent the world, how they decompose problems, how they generalize from a handful of examples, most of that is locked inside someone's head. You can run behavioral experiments, you can look at neural data, but it's all pretty indirect. Language is different. When someone explains how to do something, or gives you a set of instructions, or describes a plan, they're externalizing a representation that was presumably doing real work internally. And it's compositional, it's discrete, it has this structure you can get your hands on. So it felt like the richest available window into the kinds of abstractions people are actually using.

The other piece is that language is clearly not just a readout. It feeds back in. Kids who learn the word for a category get better at distinguishing that category. People who are given a verbal rule learn tasks faster than people who have to discover the rule from trial and error. So there's this two-way relationship where language is both evidence about cognition and a tool that cognition uses. That made it feel central rather than peripheral.

And from a modeling perspective, which is where I actually spend most of my time, language gave us a very concrete way to ask questions about learning. If you build a system that has to acquire some skill, and you can hand it a natural-language description of the skill, or ask it to produce one, you get a really sharp test of whether it has built the right kind of abstraction. That's turned out to be a productive way to study models, and I'd like to think it tells us something about people too.

astra-6.text:
What drew me to language was that it gives us a very concrete window into a lot of the things that make human intelligence interesting. We can take something we know, put it into words, and communicate it to somebody else, who can then use it to do something they couldn’t do before. That’s a pretty remarkable ability.

And understanding language seems to require much more than knowing how words fit together. You need knowledge about the world, some ability to reason, and some understanding of what another person knows and is trying to accomplish. So language processing felt like a way to study those broader questions about cognition while still having a concrete computational problem to work on: what would you actually have to build to get a machine to do this?

sol-6.1.text:
I think language is a really interesting window into cognition because it connects to so many other things that we do. To understand what somebody says, you often have to reason about what they know, what they want, and what’s going on in the world around them. So even though the thing you observe is a sequence of words, the process that produces it draws on a much richer set of capabilities.

And language gives us a fairly concrete way to study those capabilities computationally. You can build a model, ask it to understand or produce language, and examine where it succeeds and where it fails. That doesn’t automatically tell you how people work, but it gives you a way to make hypotheses about cognition precise and testable.
